title: The Avenue of Volcanoes: Relative Clauses

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know relative clauses with *que* and *quien* from B1 Unit 5. A relative clause adds information about a noun: *que* works for people and things, and *quien* can follow a comma when the noun is a person. This is the grammar you need to describe a landscape: which volcano, which valley, which city.

sections.title: At work on the topic
rows: Humboldt es el naturalista que visitó la región en 1802.
*que* = who: it points back to a person
El Cotopaxi es un volcán que sigue activo.
*que* = that/which: it points back to a thing
Humboldt, quien midió las montañas, dibujó las plantas por altitud.
*quien* after a comma: extra information about a person
El Chimborazo es la montaña que Humboldt intentó subir.
*que* can be the object: the mountain (that) Humboldt tried to climb

items.spanish: Quito es la ciudad que está al pie del volcán Pichincha.
items.english: Quito is the city that lies at the foot of the Pichincha volcano.

items.spanish: El páramo es un paisaje que guarda el agua.
items.english: The páramo is a landscape that stores water.

items.spanish: Humboldt, quien visitó Ecuador en 1802, dibujó las plantas por altitud.
items.english: Humboldt, who visited Ecuador in 1802, drew the plants by altitude.

items.spanish: El volcán que se ve desde Quito es el Pichincha.
items.english: The volcano you can see from Quito is the Pichincha.

sections.content: English often leaves *that* out (*the volcano we can see*). Spanish never leaves out *que*: *el volcán que vemos*. Do not repeat the noun inside the clause either: *la montaña que Humboldt intentó subir*, not *la montaña que Humboldt la intentó subir*.
